extracted.subtask_description: Standards and enforcement priorities the FTC uses to identify and challenge deceptive advertising and marketing across media, with examples of investigated practices and typical remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring advertising in all media
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC monitors advertising in all media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission actively reviews ads across offline and online channels for deceptive or unfair practices; oversight is not limited to one medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: False and unproven health or disease-prevention claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC challenges claims that products prevent disease or promote health when such claims are false or not supported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include claims that a vacuum/air purifier can prevent the flu, that a skin cream can reduce body size, and that shoes can ‘tone’ or ‘strengthen’ muscles. Enforcement typically seeks settlements requiring companies to stop making the claims and, where appropriate, to refund consumers (e.g., Reebok agreed to a $25 million refund).

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading product performance claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims about product benefits, efficacy, or performance that mislead consumers are subject to challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by cases such as Reebok EasyTone/RunTone (toning claims) and Nivea My Silhouette (slimming claims). Such claims must be substantiated; otherwise the FTC may obtain settlements, prohibitions on the claims, and consumer refunds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fake news sites and phony testimonials
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating or using fake news sites or phony testimonials to promote products is deceptive advertising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission filed suits against online marketers who created fake news sites posting fabricated testimonials touting acai berry supplements. Remedies include permanent injunctions, bans on the practices, and monetary settlements (e.g., operators ordered to pay or surrender assets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative-option programs billed without informed consumer consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Charging consumers recurring fees (negative-option billing) without first obtaining their informed consent is deceptive and actionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases against marketers such as Jesse Willms and Michael Bruce Moneymaker allege recurring charges without consent; FTC actions have banned operators from marketing negative-option programs and required surrender of assets and other relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrepresentation of service terms, quantities, fees (prepaid services)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representing service quantities, fees, or contract terms (for example, minutes of talk time on prepaid phone cards) in a way that overstates consumer value is deceptive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Millenium Telecard was challenged for allegedly false and deceptive claims about minutes of talk time and fees that reduced card value; enforcement produced a monetary settlement. Businesses must accurately disclose fees and actual service amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using novel or improper payment methods to debit consumer accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Payment processors or marketers using new/novel payment methods to debit consumers’ accounts in a deceptive or unauthorized manner can be enjoined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Landmark Clearing was the subject of FTC action banning a payment processor from using a novel payment method to debit accounts. The FTC can prohibit payment mechanisms that facilitate deceptive billing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement remedies and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: When the FTC finds deceptive or unfair practices it seeks remedies including refunds to consumers, bans on specific marketing practices, asset surrender, and prohibitions on future deceptive claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples on the page: settlements requiring refunds (Reebok), bans on marketing tactics (fake news sites, negative-option programs), payments to consumers (Central Coast Nutraceuticals $1.5M; Millenium Telecard $2.32M), and permanent injunctions against operators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking and policy action to strengthen protections (e.g., mortgage ads)
rubrics_metrics.description: The FTC undertakes rulemaking to strengthen consumer protections against categories of deceptive advertising, such as mortgage advertisements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page references a 'New Rule Strengthening Consumer Protections Against Deceptive Mortgage Advertisements,' indicating that beyond case-by-case enforcement the Commission issues rules addressing systemic ad categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer education and outreach about deceptive practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Educating consumers about common deceptive practices (e.g., free-trial misrepresentations, bogus weight-loss claims, misleading fitness gear ads) is part of the FTC's approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outreach examples include videos and consumer-education articles like 'Free Trials Aren't Always Free' and tips on buying fitness gear; such materials aim to inform consumers how to spot and avoid deceptive offers.
